papers.title: Clinical Significance and Distribution of Cerebrospinal Fluid Type IV Oligoclonal Band Pattern in Neurological Disorders: A Retrospective Analysis
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: To characterize the clinical features and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of patients exhibiting a type IV oligoclonal band (OCB) pattern, defined by the presence of identical IgG bands in both CSF and serum. Methods: This retrospective observational study included all consecutive adult patients with a type IV pattern detected during routine CSF analysis at Geneva University Hospitals in 2023. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected through chart review. Results: A total of 178 patients were included. The mean age was 60.2 years (SD 16.5), and 51.7% were female. The type IV pattern was most frequently observed in non-inflammatory neurological diseases (NIND) (n=103, 57.9%). Other inflammatory neurological diseases accounted for 37 cases (20.7%), multiple sclerosis was identified in 8 patients (4.5%), and peripheral nervous system disorders were present in 20 patients (11.2%). Systemic inflammatory comorbidities were observed in 40 patients (22.5%). An elevated albumin quotient was present in 73 patients (41%) and was most common among those with CNS infections, aseptic meningitis, CNS neoplastic diseases, and peripheral nervous system disorder. Repeated CSF analyses demonstrated temporal fluctuations in the type IV pattern in some patients, without corresponding changes in diagnosis. Discussion: The type IV pattern is predominantly associated with NIND and is relatively uncommon in multiple sclerosis. Although it may reflect systemic immune activation and/or blood brain barrier dysfunction in certain inflammatory conditions, its clinical significance remains nonspecific. These findings support cautious interpretation of the type IV pattern in routine clinical practice.

papers.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Background: Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha's predictive contribution (G) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD-HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha's carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and G each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen-Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and G can change partly independently. Results: G was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10^3G, -3.19; 95% confidence interval -5.25 to -1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and G each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in G, whereas reducing downstream input lowered G with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions: At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity identifies a prognostically distinct subgroup in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background: -synuclein (Lewy body-type) co-pathology has been identified at autopsy in a subset of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, its prevalence and prognostic relevance in vivo remain poorly characterized. Methods: We analyzed baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) -synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn SAA) status in 443 patients with ALS from two cohorts (Nagoya, Japan, n = 248; Bologna, Italy, n = 195). Samples were classified as strong-positive, weak-positive, or negative based on RT-QuIC reactivity across replicate wells, using the assay's established a priori criteria at initial and repeat testing; classifications were corroborated by quantitative kinetic parameters. We compared age- and sex-adjusted odds of positivity in ALS with those in cognitively unimpaired (CU; n = 999; stratified by amyloid-{beta} [A{beta}] status), A{beta}-positive mild cognitive impairment (n = 224), and Alzheimer's disease dementia (n = 319) groups from the Swedish BioFINDER cohort. In ALS, we examined tracheostomy-free survival and longitudinal functional decline using cohort-stratified Cox and linear mixed-effects models, respectively. We also assessed interactions between Syn SAA status and baseline CSF neurofilament light chain (NfL). Prognostic analyses were performed in sporadic ALS and repeated after including familial or genetic cases. Results: Strong Syn SAA positivity was detected in 24/443 patients with ALS (5.4%); overall positivity, including weak-positive samples, was 37/443 (8.4%). Patients with ALS did not have significantly higher odds of SAA positivity than A{beta}-negative CU participants (age- and sex-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.33, 95% CI [0.82, 2.14]) and had significantly lower odds than patients with Alzheimer's disease dementia (OR 0.44, [0.27, 0.70]). Among patients with sporadic ALS, strong Syn SAA positivity was associated with shorter tracheostomy-free survival after adjustment for established predictors including NfL (adjusted HR 2.08 [1.25, 3.45]), whereas weak positivity showed no clear survival association. In linear mixed-effects models, strong Syn SAA positivity modified the association between NfL and ALSFRS-R decline (NfL x Syn SAA x time interaction {beta} -0.70 points/month [-1.26, -0.14] per SD NfL). These findings persisted in analyses including familial or genetic ALS cases and in those restricted to A{beta}-negative patients. Neuropathological findings (n = 5) were concordant with the CSF Syn SAA classification. Conclusions: A strong -synuclein seeding profile was uncommon in ALS but identified a subgroup with shorter survival and a stronger association between NfL and functional decline. These findings provide ante-mortem evidence that -synuclein co-pathology may contribute to prognostic heterogeneity in ALS.

papers.title: Scoring the NIH Stroke Scale from bedside exam transcripts: a synthetic benchmark of a decision model and a large language model
papers.abstract: Background. Clinicians score the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at the bedside, often under time pressure, and ambient AI tools that listen to clinical encounters are now entering practice. It is not known whether software can score the NIHSS from the exam conversation itself, rather than extract a score that has already been written in a note. Methods. We created 112 synthetic code-stroke cases. One hundred were allocated in proportion to real code-stroke presentations, and 12 stress cases tested special scoring rules. For each case, a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote a reference score form (the answer key) and a speech-to-text-style exam transcript, with main-set transcripts split evenly between a narrated and a telegraphic examiner style. A second model (Claude Fable 5.1), blind to the key, scored every transcript and agreed with the key on 99.2% of items. Each transcript was then scored by Jev, a decision model, and by gpt-6-luna, a general large language model (LLM). The primary outcome was item-level accuracy against the key. Results. The LLM scored 99.0% of items correctly (95% CI 98.4-99.4) and Jev 94.4% (93.2-95.4; McNemar p < 0.001), with exact totals in 101 and 63 of 112 cases. Jev was faster (median 0.15 vs 5.78 s per exam) and cheaper (USD 0.23 vs 0.67 per 1,000 exams). With telegraphic examiners, accuracy fell from 98.0% to 90.9% for Jev and from 100% to 97.7% for the LLM. In a post-hoc analysis that kept only the examiner's words, accuracy stayed high when the examiner narrated (Jev 96.9%, LLM 98.8%) but dropped to about 80% when the examiner used shorthand. Most of Jev's errors fell on four items (language, extinction and neglect, LOC questions and visual fields), and on each it tended to repeat the same mistake, for example scoring slurred speech as aphasia. Its confidence flagged most of these errors. Re-checking the 14.8% of items with confidence below 0.70 would have caught 86% of them, and a simulated hybrid reached 98.8% accuracy. Conclusions. Both engines scored most NIHSS items correctly from exam transcripts. The LLM was more accurate, and the decision model was faster and cheaper, with a confidence signal that could route uncertain items to an LLM. Because the cases and the key are synthetic, these findings need confirmation with recorded exams and human raters.

papers.title: Hospital-treated infectious diseases, infection burden, and subsequent risk of demyelinating diseases: a prospective cohort study
papers.abstract: Abstract Background and Objectives Epstein-Barr virus infection is an established risk factor for multiple sclerosis (MS). However, associations between a wider range of infections and MS remain unclear, particularly among middle-aged and older adults. Risk factors for other (non-MS) demyelinating diseases are also poorly understood. We examined whether hospital-treated infectious diseases and infection burden were associated with subsequent risk of demyelinating diseases. Methods This prospective cohort study included 484,292 UK Biobank participants (mean age 56.5 [SD 8.1] years; 54.3% women). Participants with demyelinating diseases at baseline were excluded. Hospital-treated infectious diseases and incident demyelinating diseases were ascertained from linked inpatient records. The primary outcome was any incident demyelinating disease; secondary outcomes were MS and other demyelinating diseases (not mutually exclusive). Infection burden was assessed by episode count, maximum number of concurrent infections, and number of affected anatomical sites. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusted for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Results During a median follow-up of 12.7 years (IQR, 12.0-13.4), 592 participants (0.12%) developed demyelinating diseases, including 436 with MS and 194 with other demyelinating diseases. Hospital-treated infectious diseases were associated with higher risks of all demyelinating diseases (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.49-2.17), MS (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.51-2.35), and other demyelinating diseases (HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.18-2.31). For all demyelinating diseases, greater infection burden across all 3 measures was associated with progressively higher risk (all P for trend <0.001); HRs were 1.45 (95% CI 1.16-1.81) for 1 infection episode and 2.97 (95% CI 2.22-3.97) for [≥]2 episodes versus none. Discussion Hospital-treated infectious diseases and greater infection burden were associated with higher subsequent risk of demyelinating diseases among middle-aged and older adults. These findings broaden current understanding of infection-related risk and may inform future prevention research.

papers.title: Using Diffusion Similarity Networks to Identify, Track, and Predict Movement Disorders
papers.abstract: Characterizing individual structural brain alterations in movement disorders like Parkinsons disease (PD) and Essential Tremor (ET) remains a significant challenge in clinical neuroscience. While brain structural connectivity (SC) derived from Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) tractography maps physical white matter pathways, it fails to capture localized microstructural remodelings within gray matter structures. In this study, we use Diffusion Similarity Networks (DSNs) as a novel framework to estimate microstructural connectivity from diffusion weighted imaging (DWI). First, we evaluate the ability of DSNs to differentiate individuals with PD from healthy controls (HC). We used Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) to visualize differences between the fused networks of both groups as well as the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT) to quantify changes in network topology, including transitivity, clustering coefficient, global efficiency, and betweenness centrality. Second, to evaluate the capacity of DSNs to track disease progression over time, we utilized longitudinal data extracted from the Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database, mapping distinct functional subnetwork degeneration trajectories in PD patients. Finally, we developed a predictive Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework on a locally collected cohort to address the challenging task of differentiating PD from ET, utilizing DSNs as highly discriminant input features. Our results demonstrate that DSN metrics successfully capture distinct structural signatures that reliably separate clinical phenotypes, while longitudinal modeling reveals an accelerated, progressive decay in specific motor and basal ganglia subnetwork topologies over time. Furthermore, the GNN model achieved high classification performance (Balanced accuracy = 0.8684, AUC= 0.9420) in distinguishing PD from ET globally, with local explain- ability analysis successfully showing the specific brain Regions of Interest (ROIs) driving the differential diagnosis. Overall, these findings demonstrate that Diffusion Similarity Networks serve as a robust, non-invasive biomarker for movement disorders, offering deep insights into disease progression and an explainable AI tool for clinical decision support.

papers.title: Proteogenomics captures a midlife biological state of Alzheimer's disease susceptibility
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) develops over decades, but biological processes underlying susceptibility during midlife remain poorly understood. Using multimodal neuroimaging and plasma proteomics in UK Biobank participants, we identified circulating proteomic signatures of brain structure and organization. This 'neurostructural proteome' predicted future cognitive decline, incident dementia, and later-life AD pathology across independent cohorts spanning two decades of follow-up. Genetic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses demonstrated convergence of the neurostructural proteome and AD genetic architecture, highlighting enrichment in astrocyte, microglia, and endothelial pathways beyond the APOE region. Collectively, these findings identify a circulating neurostructural proteome detectable in midlife that captures molecular processes associated with future AD susceptibility and provide a framework for uncovering an early biological landscape of disease susceptibility that precedes conventional biomarkers and clinical onset.

papers.title: Real-world implementation and outcomes of extended-window intravenous thrombolysis in Catalonia, 2016-2024: A population-based study using the CICAT registry.
papers.abstract: Background. Evidence supporting intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) beyond 4.5 hours is based on selected populations using advanced imaging, while real-world data remains limited. We describe its uptake, selection strategies, treatment pathways, and outcomes in routine practice. Methods. We conducted a population-based observational study using the prospective multicenter CICAT registry in Catalonia, Spain (2016-2024). Patients receiving extended-window IVT (>4.5 hours or unknown onset) were grouped into IVT alone and IVT before mechanical thrombectomy (bridging therapy), with conventional-window patients as a clinical reference. Excellent functional outcome was defined as a 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-1 or return to prestroke mRS, and good functional outcome as mRS 0-2 or return to prestroke mRS. Safety outcomes were symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) and mortality. Results. Among 12,547 patients treated with IVT, 656 (5.2%) received extended-window treatment (450 IVT alone; 206 bridging therapy). The proportion treated in the extended window increased from 3.5% in 2016-2018 to 7.4% in 2022-2024, with perfusion imaging predominantly guiding patient selection (84.1%). In the IVT alone cohort, excellent functional outcome occurred in 42.8% of extended-window and 47.2% of conventional-window patients; sICH occurred in 3.6% and 2.3%, and mortality in 12.9% and 12.5%, respectively. Corresponding outcomes in the bridging cohort 40.0% and 45.1% for good functional outcome, 20.6% and 18.6% for mortality, and 5.8% and 4.1% for sICH respectively. Differences with the reference group were also generally modest among patients aged >80 years and those with prestroke disability. Conclusions. Extended-window IVT was progressively adopted across a population-based stroke network, predominantly using advanced imaging. Among selected patients, observed differences in functional and safety outcomes relative to the conventional-window reference group were generally modest, including in populations underrepresented in randomized trials. These findings should be interpreted in the context of differences in patient selection and case mix between treatment windows.

papers.title: Lesions causing room tilt illusion link a cerebello-cingulate brain network to verticality perception
authors: F. L. W. V. J. Schaper
papers.abstract: Verticality perception is the sense of one's body orientation relative to gravity. It can be disrupted by neurological diseases or during aviation and space flight, resulting in falls and accidents. This perception is thought to arise from integration of vestibular and visual signals, yet where this multisensory computation is spatially implemented in the human brain remains unresolved. Room tilt illusion (RTI), in which the visual environment abruptly reorients relative to gravity (typically by 90{degrees} or 180{degrees}), has been proposed as a model disorder for studying verticality perception. Here, we leverage focal brain lesions (predominantly ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes) causing RTI to localize this multisensory computation. We assembled a total of 37 patients with brain lesions causing RTI from a systematic literature search and local cases across two centers. Clinical data were tabulated and lesions were analyzed using multimodal voxel- and connectome-based lesion mapping methods. Lesion findings were further tested against an independent dataset of 509 direct electrical stimulation sites associated with vestibular or non-vestibular percepts. The RTI lesions were distributed across cortical and subcortical locations, with the cerebellum representing the most frequent lesion site (49%). Despite anatomical heterogeneity, lesion connectivity converged on two hub regions: one in the posterior cerebellum and another in the mid-cingulate cortex. This pattern was robust to methodological variations, separation of RTI subtypes, and exclusion of cerebellar lesions. This pattern was also specific to RTI when compared against 185 phenotypically matched lesions from patients with milder disturbances of verticality perception and 1,110 lesions associated with 27 other neuropsychiatric syndromes. Finally, independent direct electrical stimulation data converged on both lesion-derived RTI hubs (mid-cingulate cortex: g=0.62, p<.001; posterior cerebellum: g=0.34, p=.014, 10,000 label permutations). In conclusion, anatomically diverse RTI lesions localize to a specific cerebello-cingulate network, providing an anatomical framework for verticality perception in the human brain. Our findings generate testable hypotheses for experimentally modulating or protecting verticality perception in neurological patients or pilots.

papers.title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model
papers.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.

papers.title: Aspirin-Containing Antiplatelet Therapy and In-Hospital Gout Flares in Acute Ischemic Stroke Patients with Gout and Hyperuricemia: A Retrospective New-User Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background: Antiplatelet selection is challenging in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS), gout, and hyperuricemia. We compared the risk of in-hospital gout flares between aspirin-containing regimens and clopidogrel monotherapy, and examined subsequent aspirin discontinuation during dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). Methods: A retrospective new-user cohort study was conducted based on electronic medical records (2019-2025). Patients were categorized into aspirin-containing therapy (aspirin monotherapy or DAPT with aspirin plus clopidogrel) and clopidogrel monotherapy groups. The primary analysis used IPTW-adjusted logistic regression. Interaction tests assessed effect modification and a Sankey diagram visualized DAPT treatment transition. Results: Among 105,890 screened patients, 457 were enrolled (234 aspirin-containing therapy, 223 clopidogrel monotherapy). In-hospital gout flares occurred in 187 (40.9%). Aspirin-containing regimens were associated with a higher flare risk (OR = 1.57, 95% CI 1.07-2.31, P = 0.022). Results were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Higher SUA (OR 1.20 per 1-mg/dL increase, 95% CI 1.03-1.40; P = 0.023) and baseline mRS [≥]3 (OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.42-3.20; P < 0.001) were independently associated with in-hospital gout flares. No significant interactions were observed between antiplatelet regimens and SUA, mRS or urate-lowering therapy (ULT). Among DAPT recipients, aspirin discontinuation in patients with gout flares was 65.2%, 66.7%, and 56.0% in 2019-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025, respectively, versus 47.8%, 28.6%, and 11.9% in those without flares. Conclusions: In AIS patients with gout and hyperuricemia, initiating aspirin-containing regimens was associated with a higher risk of in-hospital gout flares compared with clopidogrel monotherapy. Gout flares during DAPT were accompanied by frequent aspirin discontinuation, which may limit completion of guideline-recommended DAPT. Prospective studies are needed.

papers.title: Plasma eMTBR-tau as a marker of clinical stage and progression across the Alzheimer's disease continuum
papers.abstract: Importance: Plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration may help characterise progression across the Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum. Plasma eMTBR-tau243 has been associated with tau pathology and cognitive decline. Whether plasma eMTBR-tau levels differ across subjective cognitive decline (SCD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD dementia, between MCI subtypes, or best discriminate subsequent clinical progression in brain health and memory clinic populations remains unclear. Objective: To compare plasma eMTBR-tau and selected biomarkers of neurodegeneration, neuropathology, and neuroinflammation across the AD continuum by pTau217 and APOE {epsilon}4 status, and explore their associations with clinical progression over two years. Design: Observational cohort study with longitudinal follow-up in a subset of participants. Setting: Healthy Brain Ageing (HBA) brain health and memory clinic, Sydney, Australia. Participants underwent assessment between October 2018 and April 2026. Participants: Cross-sectional analysis included 436 participants; 166 were followed up approximately two years later. Exposures: Plasma biomarker quantification using the NULISAseq Neuro 220 Panel, clinical classification by multidisciplinary memory clinic assessment, plasma pTau217 status (SIMOA ALZpath), and APOE {epsilon}4 carrier status. Main Outcomes and Measures: Fasting blood was collected on the morning of assessment. Plasma was analysed using the NULISAseq Neuro 220 panel. Relative biomarker abundance was compared across clinical and biomarker-defined groups. BD-pTau217 and eMTBR-tau levels at the preceding assessment were modelled individually and jointly to assess SCD-to-MCI progression and MCI-to-AD conversion over approximately two years of follow-up. Results: Among 436 participants (mean [SD] age, 70.2 [8.0] years; 67.2% female), 186 had SCD, 228 MCI, and 22 AD dementia. Among 221 biomarkers, phosphorylated tau analytes (pTau181/T205/T212/217/231) dominated clinical group differences, while eMTBR-tau showed the largest adjusted differences: 1.69-fold higher in MCI than SCD, 6.55-fold higher in AD than SCD and 3.88-fold higher in AD than MCI (all FDR-adjusted P < .001). eMTBR-tau was higher in multidomain amnestic MCI than in SCD, and in pTau217-positive than in pTau217-negative individuals. In the exploratory MCI-to-AD analysis (6/40 converted over 2 years), eMTBR-tau at the preceding assessment showed higher cross-validated discrimination of MCI-to-AD conversion than BD-pTau217 (AUC, 0.936 vs. 0.882). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical stages across the AD continuum are defined by a tau-dominant pattern. eMTBR-tau showed prominent stage-related differences, supporting its further evaluation as a marker of clinical progression.

papers.title: Age and sex impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity beyond symptom associations in persistent post-concussive symptoms
papers.abstract: 1.Objectiveto investigate whether resting-state EEG aperiodic parameters (i.e., offset and exponent) are associated with symptom burden and demographic factors in patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) and differ from healthy controls. MethodsIn this cross-sectional observational study, resting-state eye-closed high-density EEG was recorded in patients with PPCS and in age-matched healthy controls. Aperiodic parameters were extracted from EEG power spectra. In patients, hierarchical multiple linear regression models included age and sex as a base model, with additional demographic and clinical symptoms entered separately. Patient-control differences were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex. ResultsSeventy patients with PPCS (54 female; 39.57{+/-}12.21 y.; 109.5 [76.5; 196] days post-concussion) recruited from a concussion care pathway and 38 healthy controls (17 female; 39.61{+/-}13.57 y.) were included. In patients, younger age and male sex were associated with higher offset and exponent values (all p [≤].014). None of the additional demographic and clinical variables improved model fit beyond age and sex (all p[≥].143). After adjustment for age and sex, neither offset (p=.898) nor exponent (p=.100) differed between patients and controls. ConclusionResting-state aperiodic EEG parameters were consistently associated with age and sex, but not with self-reported symptom burden or clinical characteristics in patients with PPCS. Not accounting for these factors may generate apparent group differences attributable, at least in part, to demographic variability. SignificanceAge and sex are important sources of inter-individual variability in resting-state aperiodic EEG activity and should be systematically considered when investigating such features. HighlightsO_LIAge and sex significantly impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity. C_LIO_LIAperiodic EEG parameters were not associated with symptom burden in persistent post-concussive symptoms. C_LIO_LIAperiodic offset and exponent did not differ between patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms and healthy controls after adjustment for age and sex. C_LI

papers.title: Genetic susceptibility to Lewy body disease and the distribution of Lewy pathology
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies of Parkinsons disease and dementia with Lewy bodies largely rely on clinical diagnoses, which can misclassify cases and cannot characterise the anatomical distribution of Lewy pathology. Autopsy cohorts allow identification of variants associated both with developing Lewy body disease and with the neocortical extent of its pathology. We meta-analysed genome-wide data from 2,661 individuals of European ancestry with autopsy-confirmed Lewy body disease and 12,068 controls (2,124 autopsy-confirmed) from the Global Parkinsons Genetics Program (GP2) and the National Institutes of Health NeuroBioBank, and estimated genetic correlation with clinically diagnosed Alzheimers disease. In 2,309 cases from the GP2 and the Mayo Clinic Jacksonville Brain Bank, we compared neocortical (n = 1,362) with brainstem or limbic (n = 947) Lewy pathology, adjusting for Alzheimers disease co-pathology, age at death and sex. Under a neuropathological case definition, five established loci reached genome-wide significance: APOE4 (OR 2.27, 95% CI 2.06-2.50), GBA1 E326K (OR 2.57, 95% CI 2.01-3.28), SNCA (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.23-1.48; TMEM175 p.M393T (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.19-1.43), and HLA class II (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.61-0.79). Lead associations differed by antemortem diagnosis. Across all cases, the SNCA association was indexed by a 5 signal previously associated with dementia with Lewy bodies and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, rather than the canonical 3 Parkinsons disease variant. Among 1,216 cases diagnosed during life with Parkinsons disease, with or without dementia, the 3 variant was the lead SNCA signal, and the APOE4 effect was attenuated (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.37-1.81). Genetic correlation with Alzheimers disease (0.33, P = 0.02) persisted after excluding the APOE region (0.31, P = 0.03). Within cases, APOE4 was the only susceptibility locus associated with neocortical involvement (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.45-1.98; P = 2.5 x 10-11), including among 666 GP2 cases without significant Alzheimers disease co-pathology (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.18-2.63; P = 0.005). Each additional e4 allele was also associated with a more advanced Lewy pathology stage (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.50-2.06). Autopsy-confirmed Lewy body disease shares its major susceptibility loci with clinically defined disease. Of these, only APOE4 was also associated with neocortical involvement, independently of measured Alzheimers disease co-pathology, suggesting that it influences not only whether Lewy pathology develops but how far it extends.

papers.title: Racial Disparities and Trends in Alzheimers and Parkinsons Disease-Related Mortality: A CDC WONDER Study 2018-2024
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective: The objectives of this study were to examine racial differences and temporal trends in Alzheimer's disease (AD)- and Parkinson's disease (PD)-related mortality among U.S. adults and to assess whether racial mortality patterns and temporal changes differed. Methods: We analyzed CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death data from 2018-2024, where mortality was defined as deaths with AD or PD recorded as an underlying or contributing cause. Age-standardized mortality rates and adjusted mortality rate ratios (MRRs) were estimated. Joint-point regression evaluated racial differences, annual percentage changes (APCs), and disease-race-year interactions. Sensitivity analyses assessed the robustness of the findings. Results: Black had significantly lower PD-related mortality than White (adjusted mortality rate ratios [MRRs]: 0.62-0.69; all p<0.001), whereas AD-related mortality showed no significant racial differences (MRRs: 0.91-1.06). Compared with 2018, mortality increased significantly in 2020 for both diseases among White adults (AD: MRR=1.21; PD: MRR=1.27) and Black adults (AD: MRR=1.27; PD: MRR=1.37), followed by partial declines. PD-related mortality increased significantly among White adults during 2018-2023 (annual percentage change [APC]=3.08%; 95% CI: 1.15%-5.05%), whereas trends among Black adults (APC=3.51%; 95% CI: -2.94% to 10.39%) and AD-related mortality trends in both racial groups were not statistically significant. The disease-race-year interaction was not significant (p=0.942), indicating insufficient evidence that temporal mortality patterns differed jointly. Conclusions: Recorded PD-related mortality was lower among Black than White adults, whereas AD-related mortality showed no statistically significant racial difference. These findings support disease-specific mortality surveillance and further investigation of potential differences in diagnostic recognition and death-certificate documentation.

papers.title: A digital biomarker of white-matter routing from diffusion MRI as an early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed after a decade-long phase in which pathology accumulates; current markers show that pathology is present, but not how far it has advanced. Because white-matter structure is altered early, we computed two graph-theoretic indices of periventricular white-matter routing from diffusion MRI in 1,706 OASIS-3 sessions: the Route Concordance Index (RCI), a population-calibrated path-concordance score over 316 routes, and a global conductance from the connectome's graph Laplacian. RCI was reduced before clinical conversion and declined monotonically across a five-stage trajectory (cross-validated AUC = 0.817 for stable-CN vs. pre-AD; comparable to hippocampal volume and exceeding entorhinal thickness, global conductance, and DTI-ALPS), with degradation concentrated in fronto-striatal circuits. A classifier combining these routing features with demographic, structural-MRI and cognitive covariates detected conversion to MCI or AD up to four years before diagnosis (AUC = 0.831; 0.918 within one year; modest positive predictive value). Findings replicated in ADNI (n = 609; conductance AUC = 0.805; RCI = 0.797 under frozen external validation) and tracked CSF amyloid-beta 42 in the expected direction. Computed from a standard diffusion MRI sequence, RCI is comparable to established structural and demographic biomarkers on preclinical discrimination while, unlike them, declining cleanly and monotonically across the disease trajectory, supporting prospective validation for risk stratification.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomic Correlates of Cognitive Function in Older Adults From Central Africa
papers.abstract: Importance: Blood based proteomic biomarkers may support scalable dementia research, but their associations with cognitive phenotype remain poorly characterized in sub Saharan African populations. Objective: To examine associations between selected plasma proteins and multidomain cognitive performance in older adults in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Design: Cross sectional secondary analysis of baseline data from the Etude du Vieillissement Cognitif et de Demence en Republique Democratique du Congo (EVCD RDC), with participant recruitment and data collection from July 2024 through September 2025. Setting: Community based prospective cohort in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo. Participants: The analytic sample included 779 participants: 143 cognitively unimpaired, 218 with mild cognitive impairment, 203 with Alzheimer disease, and 215 with other dementia. Median age was 73 years (IQR, 70 to 78); 495 participants (63.5%) were female and 284 (36.5%) were male. Exposures: Plasma abundance of 10 candidate proteins measured using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120. Candidates were selected from an earlier panel wide analysis based on cognitively unimpaired vs Alzheimer disease discrimination and false discovery rate adjusted significance. Main Outcomes and Measures: Seven cognitive outcomes spanning global cognition, language, working memory, learning, delayed memory, mental abstraction, and problem solving. Separate linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, current smoking, education, and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Benjamini Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied within each cognitive outcome across the 10 proteins. Results: Eighteen protein cognition associations were nominally significant, and 6 remained significant after correction. Higher MME was associated with better language, global cognition, and delayed memory. Higher NEFL was associated with poorer global cognition and delayed memory. Higher ENO2 was associated with better delayed memory. No p tau217 based measure remained significant after correction. Conclusions and Relevance: MME and NEFL showed the most consistent associations with cognitive performance, whereas ptau217 based measures did not survive multiple testing correction. Biomarkers optimized for Alzheimer pathology detection may differ from those most closely associated with cross sectional cognitive phenotype, supporting population specific evaluation of plasma proteomic markers.

papers.title: Cognitive Trajectories of Post-Stroke Delirium: Longitudinal Global and Domain-Specific Impairment and Digital Markers
papers.abstract: BackgroundPoststroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) and poststroke delirium (PSD) remain underexplored. Longitudinal assessments of cognition before PSD onset and at follow-up are scarce, leaving the association between PSD and subsequent global and domain-specific PSCI unclear. Digital assessments using task-derived kinematic parameters may provide complementary insights into cognitive vulnerability and PSD risk. MethodsIn this prospective longitudinal study, patients with acute stroke underwent multidomain tablet-based neuropsychological assessment within the acute phase, before PSD onset, and at 90 days post-stroke. Global PSCI (gPSCI) and domain-specific PSCI (attention and processing speed, executive functions, verbal memory, language, and visuospatial-construction) were assessed using norm-referenced cognitive performance. Cognitive outcomes were compared between patients with and without PSD at both time points. Functional outcome, mortality, and quality of life were assessed at 90 days. Exploratory random forest analyses evaluated the discriminatory ability of acute-phase task-derived kinematic parameters. ResultsAmong 31 patients with stroke, 10 developed PSD, 18 served as controls, and 3 dropped out. At 90 days, patients with PSD had more severe gPSCI than controls (U=19.500, p<0.001), whereas the acute-phase difference was not significant (U=50.500, p=0.057). Domain-specific analyses revealed distinct temporal patterns of cognitive impairment. During the acute phase, patients with subsequent PSD, showed significantly more severe impairments in attention and processing speed (U=29.500; p=0.003) and visuospatial-construction (U=31.500; p=0.004). At 90 days, differences in attention and processing speed persisted (U=21.000, p <0.001) with additional significant differences in executive functions (U=38.500, p=0.012) and language (U=45.500, p=0.031). Kinematic parameters showed discriminatory performance comparable to gPSCI (78.89% versus 81.50%). At 90 days, PSD was also associated with worse functional outcome (U=31.500, p=0.004), higher mortality (p=0.037), and lower mental quality of life (p=0.021). ConclusionsPSD is associated with more severe global PSCI at 90 days post-stroke and distinct temporal pattern of domain-specific PSCI. Task-derived kinematic parameters may complement conventional cognitive scores. Larger multicenter studies are needed to validate these findings. Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06680336. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06680336

papers.title: Radiological Phenotypes of Acute Brain Injury During Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation on Ultra-Low-Field Portable MRI
papers.abstract: Background: Despite the clinical importance of acute brain injury (ABI) during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), the mechanism of ECMO-associated ABI remains poorly understood, partly because conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is incompatible with ECMO devices. Ultra-low-field portable MRI (ULF-pMRI) enables high-quality bedside neuroimaging during ECMO. We aimed to characterize imaging phenotypes of ABI and explore mechanisms underlying lesion distribution across ECMO configurations. Methods: In this multicenter retrospective observational study, adults receiving ECMO who underwent bedside ULF-pMRI at Johns Hopkins University and University of Texas?Houston from December 2021 to May 2026 were included. ABI was defined as ischemic stroke (IS), intraparenchymal hemorrhage (IPH), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or subdural hematoma (SDH). Lesions were characterized according to vascular territory, cortical/subcortical lesion versus deep white matter (WM)/basal ganglia (BG) involvement, laterality, lesion burden, and cerebral small-vessel disease (SVD) using Fazekas scale. Associations between ECMO configuration (central venoarterial [VA], peripheral VA, and venovenous [VV]), echocardiographic findings, and ECMO parameters were examined. Results: Among 70 patients analyzed (55.9 {+/-} 16.2 years; 54.3% male), 29 (41.4%) had ABI. IS was the predominant type of ABI (82.8%), with most strokes affecting the frontal lobe (48.3%). All the central VA-ECMO patients with ABI demonstrated predominantly cortical/subcortical lesions, whereas deep WM/BG involvement was more frequent in peripheral VA-ECMO (53.8%). Peripheral VA-ECMO demonstrated left hemispheric predominance (85% vs. 15% right-sided, P=0.002), and deep WM/BG lesions in peripheral were associated with higher ECMO pump flow and lower pulse pressure. Among VV-ECMO patients, bilateral lesions were more common (62.5%), with a high prevalence of deep WM/BG involvement (62.5%) and SVD (75%). Conclusions: ULF-pMRI revealed distinct radiological phenotypes of ABI across ECMO configurations; cortical/subcortical lesions in central VA-ECMO, left-sided predominance in peripheral VA-ECMO and frequent deep WM/BG in VV-ECMO. These findings generate mechanistic hypotheses regarding configuration-specific pathways of ABI.

papers.title: Greater scaling and less flexible timing of cortical responses during challenging reactive balance after stroke
papers.abstract: BackgroundCortical N1 responses to balance perturbations are larger and earlier with increasing magnitude and differ with reactive stepping. Whether stroke alters this modulation is unknown. ObjectiveTo compare N1 modulation across perturbation magnitudes and reactive balance outcomes in older adults with and without stroke. We hypothesized that people with stroke would show greater N1 scaling than controls; that larger N1s at small perturbations would limit scaling (a recruitment ceiling); and that stroke would constrain N1 modulation by stepping outcome. MethodsSixteen people with chronic stroke (66{+/-}11 years) and 15 age-similar controls (68{+/-}8 years) received forward support-surface perturbations at a small standardized magnitude and at individual step thresholds ([~]50% unintentional steps). N1 peak amplitude and latency were compared across magnitudes in feet-in-place trials, and between stepping and feet-in-place trials at step threshold. N1 scaling was the relative amplitude increase between magnitudes. ResultsDespite lower clinical balance after stroke (p<0.001), step thresholds were similar between groups. N1s were larger with shorter latencies at step threshold in both groups (p<0.001), but scaled more after stroke (44% vs 13%,p=0.009). Greater scaling was associated with smaller small-magnitude N1s after stroke ({beta}=-0.43, p=0.041) and higher step thresholds across groups ({beta}=0.35, p=0.048). N1 latency was 11 ms longer in stepping trials in controls but not after stroke (interaction p=0.024). ConclusionsScaling of cortical recruitment with increasing perturbation magnitude may support reactive balance, and may be an adaptive mechanism for people after stroke. Less flexible N1 timing after stroke may limit cortical tuning to balance recovery strategy.

papers.title: Live Birth Rates Among Women With Multiple Sclerosis in Sweden, 2004 to 2022: A Population-Based Registry Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundWomen with multiple sclerosis (MS) have fewer children than other women, but whether this narrowed as pregnancy evidence became reassuring and treatment options expanded is uncertain. ObjectiveTo compare live birth trends from 2004 to 2022 between women with MS and all Swedish women. MethodsLinking the Swedish MS, National Patient, and Medical Birth Registers with national statistics, we compared age-standardised live birth rates, counted expected births at national rates, and estimated adjusted annual live-birth risk ratios in a matched comparison sample. ResultsWomen with MS (n=10,452; 76,989 woman-years) had 3,577 children, about 1,200 (25%) fewer than expected (observed-to-expected ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.77). Standardised rate ratios were below 1 annually (median 0.77). Observed-to-expected ratios were 0.73 (0.68 to 0.79) in 2004 to 2008 and 0.70 (0.65 to 0.75) in 2019 to 2022 (population-by-period interaction p=0.31). Age- and region-adjusted risk ratios ranged from 0.75 to 0.86 across periods (heterogeneity p=0.020), closest to 1 in 2009 to 2013. ConclusionWomen with MS had about one quarter fewer live births than other Swedish women, and the difference was similar in the first and last periods.

papers.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy and Disability Progression in Women with Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundEvidence on menopausal hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and disability progression in women with multiple sclerosis (MS) is limited, particularly in the era of high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy. We estimated the association between systemic HRT and sustained disability progression and recurring relapses in a contemporary national cohort. MethodsIn a nationwide Swedish registry-based cohort, we followed women with MS aged 40 to 60 years entering from 2006 through 2024, with follow-up through 2025, under a new-user design. Systemic HRT was modeled as time-varying current use and quarterly oral-equivalent dose categories. Outcomes were sustained Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) 4.0, sustained EDSS 6.0, and recurring relapses. Cox models adjusted for baseline covariates and time-varying age and disease-modifying therapy (DMT) class. ResultsAmong 7,623 women, 1,192 (15.6%) initiated HRT. Current HRT use was associated with a lower hazard of sustained EDSS 4.0 (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 0.96) but not sustained EDSS 6.0 (aHR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.16) or recurring relapses (aHR 1.00, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.36). Dose categories showed no consistent gradient. Raising the cohort-entry age floor to 50 years gave a consistent EDSS 4.0 estimate (aHR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.95). ConclusionsHRT was not associated with increased relapse risk or severe disability progression. The lower hazard of sustained EDSS 4.0 was not mirrored at EDSS 6.0 and showed no dose gradient. Given menopausal status was unmeasured, replication in cohorts with verified menopausal status is required for clear clinical interpretation.

papers.title: More tests, higher scores: Testing frequency and SDMT differences between natalizumab and rituximab
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) measures information processing speed, and repeated testing can increase scores through practice effects. However, how differences in testing frequency bear on comparisons between disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) in real-world cohorts has not been fully explored. ObjectiveTo compare SDMT trajectories between natalizumab and rituximab users and quantify the association of the testing process with those trajectories. MethodsUsing the Swedish MS Registry, we studied adults with relapsing-remitting MS initiating natalizumab or rituximab (2010-2024) with [≥]2 on-treatment SDMT assessments. Mixed-effects models with restricted cubic spline time were sequentially adjusted; log cumulative test number was the practice-effect adjustment. ResultsAmong 2,458 individuals, natalizumab initiators were tested twice as often as rituximab initiators (1.6 vs. 0.8 tests/year). The predicted natalizumab-minus-rituximab SDMT difference at 3 years was 7.0 points (95% CI 5.7-8.3) unadjusted and 1.6 (0.7-2.6) after full adjustment including cumulative test number; at 1 year it fell from 4.4 (3.3-5.4) to -0.3 (-1.2 to 0.6). ConclusionAdjustment for cumulative test number substantially attenuated the SDMT difference between natalizumab and rituximab, leaving a small residual difference of uncertain clinical importance and underscoring the need to account for testing frequency in real-world comparisons.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

papers.title: EEG Biomarkers for Rett Syndrome: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with Explainable AI
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by abnormal cortical activity, which can be captured using electroencephalography (EEG). Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise for diagnosing several neurological conditions, comprehensive evaluation of classical ML and deep learning (DL) methods, together with physiologically meaningful explanations, remains limited for RTT. This study analyses resting-state, eyes-closed EEG recordings from RTT patients and healthy controls using both power spectral density (PSD)-based ML and end-to-end DL frameworks. Classical ML models, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were trained on PSD features, while EEG-specific DL architectures, including ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, EEGNet, and EEG Conformer, were trained directly on preprocessed EEG signals. Subjectwise cross-validation was used to avoid data leakage, with balanced accuracy as the primary performance metric because it equally accounts for sensitivity and specificity. Random Forest achieved the best performance among the classical ML models, whereas EEGNet achieved the highest DL performance. An ablation study indicated that 4-second EEG epochs offered the optimal trade-off between model performance and robustness. Model interpretability was investigated using SHAP for Random Forest and occlusion sensitivity analysis for EEGNet. Both methods consistently identified delta and theta oscillations, along with centro-frontal brain regions, as key contributors to RTT classification. These findings show that both PSD-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning methods can reliably identify RTT and highlight common neurophysiological biomarkers, offering an interpretable framework for EEG-based diagnosis and biomarker discovery for Rett Syndrome.

papers.title: Cortical physiological arousal following termination of absence seizures
papers.abstract: Although the brain state preceding and during absence seizures has been well-characterized, the postictal brain state remains largely unexplored due to the prevailing assumption that absence seizures have minimal or no postictal changes. To address this gap, scalp EEG recordings from 55 patients with 3-4 Hz spike-wave discharges across four multi-site cohorts were analyzed. Spectral power was measured relative to each seizures preictal baseline, and the postictal period was compared to a time-matched preictal window. Rather than an immediate return to baseline after seizure offset, a significant broadband increase in EEG power was observed in the gamma (>25 Hz) and delta (<4 Hz) frequency bands, followed by a gradual decline over the next 15 s to 30 s. In contrast, no comparable change preceded the seizures. This suggests that recovery from an absence seizure is an active process with a characteristic electrophysiological signature consistent with cortical activation and arousal. Thus, postictal arousal may facilitate exit from the seizure state, and with further work could serve as an electrophysiological marker and therapeutic target for recovery in absence epilepsy.

papers.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Across Sleep Disorders and Its Cognitive Implications
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), sleep deprivation (SD), and narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), are associated with cognitive dysfunction and an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease. Glymphatic transport disruption has been suggested as one potential mechanistic link. However, evidence across sleep disorders and glymphatic-related metrics remains fragmented. We aimed to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical and preclinical studies to determine whether glymphatic-related metrics are altered in OSA, SD, and NT1. Across studies of OSA, glymphatic-related metrics indicated significant impairment of glymphatic transport with a moderate negative association between apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index (r=-0.53, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.63 to -0.41; p<0.001). Available evidence did not demonstrate statistically significant alterations in glymphatic measures in SD or NT1. These findings suggest that impaired glymphatic transport may represent a potential pathway linking OSA to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative risk. However, current evidence is insufficient to determine whether comparable alterations occur in SD or NT1. Substantial heterogeneity across studies highlights the need for standardized reporting and harmonized methodologies to advance the field.

papers.title: Movement-specific effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation over premotor and parietal cortices after stroke
papers.abstract: BackgroundTranscranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been proposed to support post-stroke motor recovery, but the response may depend on the task and motor-network status. We aimed to compare how premotor and parietal stimulation affects performance across reach directions with different movement demands, in preparation for therapeutic application of TMS. Methods16 participants with chronic subcortical stroke performed planar reaches with the KINARM exoskeleton toward distal and proximal targets. Before movement, a 10-Hz triple-pulse TMS train was delivered over bilateral dorsal or ventral premotor cortex (PMd, PMv) or dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (PPC) at subthreshold and suprathreshold intensities. The parietal midline was used as the control target. Participant-level bootstrap confidence intervals assessed changes in trajectory straightness and smoothness relative to the control target and differences between reach directions. We compared motor-network activity and connectivity using task-based and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from participants with stroke and neurologically intact controls. To explore response variability, we tested associations between TMS response and motor impairment, resting-state connectivity, and the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement. ResultsSuprathreshold PMd and PPC stimulation in both hemispheres improved trajectory straightness or smoothness during distal reaches relative to the control target. Suprathreshold contralesional PMd stimulation increased trajectory deviation and reduced smoothness during proximal reaches. Baseline performance during distal reaches was more closely related to motor impairment, and contralesional PMd effects were more favorable during distal than proximal reaches across all kinematic measures. Participants with stroke showed lower bilateral PMv activation during movement and stronger interhemispheric PPC connectivity. Only the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement was related to TMS response. Smaller changes relative to controls were associated with more favorable kinematic effects during distal reaches. ConclusionsMovements more affected after stroke were the most responsive to this type of stimulation. The response to TMS was also associated with task-evoked activity differences at the stimulated region between movement planning and execution. Neuromodulation may therefore be most effective when designed around both the pathophysiology of the cortical target and the type of movement. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04286516. Registered 21 January 2020.

papers.title: Amyloid and Tau Neuropathologic Stage, Coexisting Brain Disease, and Cognitive Status in a Population-Based Autopsy Cohort
papers.abstract: ImportanceInterpreting an amyloid or tau biomarker result requires knowing how often the target pathology is present in the tested population, whether a single marker characterizes the joint amyloid-tau state, and whether the detected pathology explains the patient symptoms. Population-based autopsy data addressing these questions are scarce, and recent population-scale prevalence estimates rest on biomarkers rather than ground-truth tissue examination. ObjectiveTo estimate stage-resolved, age- and sex-specific frequencies of amyloid and tau neuropathology in an unselected, admixed, autopsy population and to evaluate their clinical expression in relation to coexisting neuropathology. Design Setting and ParticipantsCross-sectional clinicopathologic study of decedents accrued from 2004 through 2025 at the Biobank for Aging Studies of the University of Sao Paulo, sampled through the centralized Sao Paulo municipal autopsy service, which performs approximately 15 000 autopsies annually and verifies about 16% of deaths in the city. Eligible decedents were aged 18 years or older with complete amyloid, tau, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and coexisting pathology assessments. ExposuresAge, sex, Thal amyloid phase, Braak neurofibrillary tangle stage, Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer Disease (CERAD) neuritic plaque score, and contributing coexisting neuropathology. Main Outcomes and MeasuresThe complete Thal phase by Braak stage distribution; age- and sex-specific frequency of pathology in the biomarker-detectable range, prespecified as Thal phase 3 to 5 together with Braak stage IV to VI; and associations with CDR and CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB). ResultsAmong 2711 decedents (mean [SD] age, 73.4 [14.4] years; range, 23 to 111 years; 1340 [49.4%] female), 531 (19.6%) met both thresholds, 270 (10.0%) the amyloid threshold only, 207 (7.6%) the tau threshold only, and 1703 (62.8%) neither. Frequency of the combined state rose from 0% at ages 23 to 50 years to 5.5% at 61 to 70, 14.5% at 71 to 80, 36.5% at 81 to 90, and 45.9% at 91 to 111 years. The proportion with CDR greater than 0 increased monotonically across Braak stages, from 88 of 541 (16.3%) at stage 0 to 155 of 179 (86.6%) at stage VI. When the combined amyloid-tau state was cross-classified with contributing coexisting pathology, CDR greater than 0 was present in 225 of 1467 participants (15.3%) with neither, 204 of 349 (58.5%) with coexisting pathology alone, 216 of 339 (63.7%) with combined amyloid-tau pathology alone, and 165 of 192 (85.9%) with both. In a multivariable model of CDR-SB, contributing coexisting pathology had the largest unique adjusted contribution (partial R2, 0.088; 95% CI, 0.064-0.114), and Braak stage had the largest share of total explained variance (Lindeman, Merenda, and Gold contribution, 0.115). Conclusions and RelevanceAmyloid and tau pathology within the range detected by current biomarkers was uncommon before age 70 and discordant in 17.6% of decedents. Contributing coexisting brain disease, which amyloid and tau biomarkers do not detect, accompanied cognitive impairment as often as advanced Alzheimer disease pathology did. These tissue-based frequencies can inform the interpretation of positive and negative biomarker results. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSAmong people with amyloid and tau neuropathology at levels expected to be detectable by current biomarkers, how often is cognitive impairment present, and how does coexisting brain disease affect this relationship? FindingsIn this cross-sectional study of 2711 autopsies from a population-based cohort aged 23 to 111 years, 19.6% had neuropathology meeting both amyloid and tau thresholds expected to be detectable by current biomarkers, rising from 0% before age 51 to 45.9% after age 90. Contributing coexisting brain disease alone was accompanied by impairment in 58.5% of participants, nearly as often as amyloid and tau pathology alone (63.7%). MeaningAge-specific neuropathologic frequencies provide an autopsy-derived context for interpreting the predictive value of Alzheimer disease biomarkers, while coexisting brain disease was a major contributor to cognitive impairment beyond amyloid and tau pathology.

papers.title: High-Density Surface Electromyography Detects Fiber-Type-Related Profiles and Disease-Relevant Fatigue Trajectories in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Fiber-type composition contributes to contractile behavior and fatigue resistance. Characterizing these physiological differences could help study and monitor disease-related changes. Direct fiber-type measurement requires biopsy, whereas animal findings may not fully translate to humans. High-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) may offer repeatable, noninvasive assessment. We recorded HD-sEMG from tibialis anterior (TA) and soleus, muscles with contrasting fast- and slow-twitch-like physiology, during sustained contractions at 30% and 50% maximum voluntary contraction in participants with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; n = 7) and healthy controls (n = 10). Given fast-fatigable motor unit vulnerability in ALS models, we compared TA-soleus profiles and fatigue-related changes. Amplitude, spectral, motor unit firing, and motor unit action potential (MUAP) features were quantified in the first 10 s of stable contraction, with firing and MUAP features derived from decomposition. Exploratory fatigue analyses assessed early-to-late changes and trajectories. Early-window root mean square (RMS), spectral power, firing rate, and MUAP amplitude were higher in TA than soleus in both groups. Group x Muscle interactions were nonsignificant. Despite higher early values, TA showed larger fatigue-related declines in high-frequency power, RMS, and firing rate than soleus, particularly in ALS-affected TA. These findings suggest HD-sEMG detects muscle-type-related electrophysiological differences, with ALS-related changes more evident during fatigue.
